name: The Fate of Tlemcen
outcome: Tlemcen made a fiefdom of Morocco
note: Morocco's war, begun two years before the campaign. Granada answered Morocco's call three days before it ended, and lost no one.

name: The Moroccan War on Castile
outcome: Defeat for Morocco: it gives up all its land on the Iberian side of the Strait (Trent's account).
note: Tunis and its vassals (Tripoli, Gabès, Gafsa, Touggourt, Bijaya) joined Morocco on 9 November 1338. Castile won the first five battles; Morocco took the sixth at Shalūqa in June 1339, and Tlemcen held al-Karash in August. Morocco's side holds Ishbīliyya and the whole Murcia area (Mursiyya, Siyāsa, Qarṭājanna, Lawraqa, Mūla); Trent's account has Tunisian troops taking Murcia. Granada can still be called in and has not been.

name: The War on Aragon
goal: Reclaim Andalusia (Granada's casus belli against Aragon)
outcome: Victory: Aragon cedes thirteen locations south of Castellón and Teruel, from Balansiyya and Shāṭiba to Uryūla and Jumalla, and pays war reparations for ten years
note: Declared on 24 May 1339 (confirmed by the save). Majorca, Navarre and Cagliari joined Aragon at once. Morocco and Tunis can be called in and have not been. The first fighting was a skirmish at Jumalla in August; on 8 November Ibn al-Khaṭīb won a great victory at Uryūla (Orihuela), worth 25 war score (Trent's screenshots), and laid siege to the town. Uryūla fell on 30 May 1340, as Castile laid siege to Mursiyya and cut the road home (Trent's account). Peace was made on 11 August 1340. Trent's account: with Aragon's field army down to some 6,000 against our 16,000, and our own supply in doubt, the sultan threatened to march on Barcelona; Aragon conceded everything south of Castellón de la Plana and Teruel, with a large indemnity.

name: The Second Moroccan War on Castile
note: Six years after its defeat of 1340, Morocco declares war again under the game's scripted Marinid casus belli to reclaim al-Andalus. Castile's alliances bring in Portugal and Aragon, with Majorca and Cagliari, so all three crowns of Iberia stand together. Tafilalt, Touat and Tlemcen march with Morocco at once; Tunis and its marches (Tripoli, Gabès, Gafsa, Bijaya and the Sahel) join on 18 October. Granada, Castile's tributary and alone on the Iberian shore, answered the call on 18 October and brought the Ṭāʾifa of Balansiyya with it; going to war with its overlord suspended the tributary bond. The Volunteers of the Faith rose again under Yaḥyā Raḥḥū (saves of 18 October and 8 November 1346; Trent's account). Tripoli, Gafsa and the Sahel had left Morocco's side by July 1348. Portugal made a separate peace on 2 September 1348, annulling its treaties with Castile for ten years and paying reparations (Trent's screenshot). On 27 January 1349 Castile, broken by the plague, made a separate peace with Granada alone, the Peace of Qurṭuba: Granada took 23 locations from Qurṭuba and Ishbīliyya to Jayyān, the Ṭāʾifa of Mursiyya took the Murcia area, Castile paid reparations and annulled its treaties with Aragon, and Granada returned to the name of Castile's tributary. Morocco fought on. Aragon made peace on 8 December 1350, giving Morocco the Balearic Islands and letting Tunis take Aragon's Sardinian vassal, the County of Cagliari, as its own subject; Majorca's lands on the mainland passed to Aragon on 1 January 1351. With Castile at the tipping point, Granada sold its promise not to fund the Marīnids for Qarmūna and the silver mines of Qusanṭīna, ceded on 21 May 1351. On 3 June Morocco surrendered to Castile, and the peace annulled Morocco's treaties with Granada (save of 3 June 1351; Trent's account).
outcome: Morocco surrenders to Castile (3 June 1351), keeping the Balearics but losing its alliance with Granada; Granada had already won the Peace of Qurṭuba (1349) and Qarmūna and Qusanṭīna (1351)

name: The Revolt of the Kingdom of Sevilla
goal: Independence for the Kingdom of Sevilla
note: The Castilian peasants of the lands won at the Peace of Qurṭuba and in 1351 rose and declared a Kingdom of Sevilla, taking all 25 of those locations (Qurṭuba, Ishbīliyya, Jayyān, Qarmūna, Qusanṭīna and the rest) in a war of independence. Qashtāla, Granada's overlord, joined on Granada's side, with the ṭāʾifas of Balansiyya and Mursiyya (save of 2 February 1353; Trent's account). The rebels raise few men (their manpower is about 360 against Granada's 3,100), but they hold the land. Granada crushed the rising before the Castilians could arrive: the rebels broke against the Granadan army at Sharīsh on 6 June, and their last army of 2,100 was destroyed at Shalūqa al-Kubrā on 27 June (save of 3 July 1353). The revolt ended on 5 July 1353: Qashtāla reaffirmed the old border, and all 25 locations returned to Granada (save of 5 July 1353).
outcome: The revolt is crushed: Granada destroys the rebel armies before Castile's arrive, and at the peace Castile reaffirms the border of the Peace of Qurṭuba; all 25 locations return to Granada (5 July 1353)

name: The Marīnid War for the Submission of Granada
goal: Morocco demands Granada's submission as its subject
note: Morocco declared war on Granada on 26 June 1360 under the Battle for the Strait's casus belli to demand Andalusī submission (the game calls it the First War for the Submission), with its subjects Tlemcen, Tafilalt and Touat. Granada is the target; Qashtāla joined as Granada's overlord and Portugal through its pact with Qashtāla. Qashtāla had only 87 men in its manpower pool after its war in Arghūn. The war allows up to 75% war score from battles. It came a year before Granada had meant to re-ally with Morocco for a war of independence, and despite relations of +150 (save of 26 June 1360; Trent's account). By June 1362 every attempt on Granada had failed: Granadan armies beat the landings at al-Mariyya (7 November 1360), Sharīsh (23 March 1361) and twice before Ishbīliyya (13 December 1361, 8 April 1362). Elsewhere the Marīnids ranged deep into Castile, breaking Castilian armies at El Escorial and Cáceres, and their and Tilimsān's fleets ruled the sea (save of 10 June 1362). About June 1362 Granada made a separate white peace with Morocco under threat of throwing its full weight into the war, with Morocco promising to respect Granada's territory; Castile and Portugal were left to fight on (Trent's account).
outcome: For Granada: a separate white peace (about June 1362), with Morocco's promise to respect its lands. The war between Morocco and Castile goes on

name: The War of Independence
note: On 20 May 1363, the day the truce with Castile ran out, Granada went to war for its independence and the amir marched north. The court had begun the claim on 31 December 1361; the casus belli the game gives is 'reclaim al-Andalus'. Castile came to it with only 183 men in its pool and 58 towns, Toledo among them, occupied by the Marīnids, with whom its war went on (Aragon now on Castile's side there). Portugal, which had made its own peace with Morocco, stood with Castile; the court's first aim was to knock it out of the war (save of 20 May 1363; Trent's account). The ṭāʾifas of Balansiyya and Mursiyya came to it untouched, having been kept out of the Marīnid war. Aragon joined Castile against Granada on 27 July 1363. Valencia and Murcia march with Granada; the Mamlūks could be called. On 1 August 1363 Yūsuf I died at Ayamonte on the march into Portugal; the war passed to his son Saʿd and the regent Naṣr al-Istijjī. Saʿd's army struck first into Portugal and laid siege to Lisbon, but the Portuguese army was not there. In the east Portugal and Aragon had joined forces and twice beaten the ṭāʾifas, at Cañete (1 March 1364) and Castellón de la Plana (5 April). The Granadan army marched east and chased them halfway across Iberia. It caught them at Zafra, Castilian land held by the Marīnids, and broke them on 3 August. It then destroyed what was left of the Portuguese and the Aragonese, one after the other, before Lisbon on 10 and 11 September (save of 11 September 1364; Trent's account). Portugal made a separate peace that same day, 11 September 1364. It gave up thirteen towns of the Algarve and the lower Alentejo, 83,000 people, which the court means to make a vassal state once the war is won. Castile and Aragon fight on. The ṭāʾifas held the line in the east: Valencia beat off an Aragonese squadron in the gulf of Valencia (25 September 1364) and a raid at Tortosa (9 March 1365), but the Murcian host was destroyed at Cuenca (27 June 1365) (autosave of 1 July 1365; Trent's account). Murād beat the Aragonese again at Cañete on 14 July 1365, and Aragon made its own peace on 2 September. On 6 January 1366 he destroyed the last Castilian army in the field, under the renegade Ibn al-Khaṭīb, at San Clemente. Castile made peace on 5 April 1366 (saves of 5 April 1366).
outcome: Victory. Granada declared its independence from Castile. Portugal (11 September 1364) gave up the Algarve and the lower Alentejo, thirteen towns. Aragon (2 September 1365) paid reparations. Castile (5 April 1366) gave up Niebla and Huelva, six towns. All three are to pay reparations for ten years. The game put Granada back under Castile as a tributary after the peace; Trent will remove that with the console.

name: The Mamlūk War on Cilicia
goal: Conquer a province of Cilicia (the Mamlūk sultan's casus belli from his council)
note: The Mamlūks, Granada's allies since 1349, went to war with Armenian Cilicia on 18 June 1364 with their subjects, and Granada and its ṭāʾifas were drawn in as allies. It is a war at the far end of the sea, fought in the middle of Granada's own (save of 11 September 1364).
outcome: Mamlūk victory. Twelve Cilician towns passed to the Mamlūks on 13 July 1365 (save of 5 April 1366, from the towns' change of owner).
